body.head: LEAVES OF GRASS. By Walt Whitman: Brooklyn, New York.
body.p:
THE sooner we give up our old opinions concerning poets and poetry, the better. Maud and Hiawatha have, let the truth break gently on us, but a new American production, Leaves of Grass, by Walt Whitman has brought us to eternal daylight and no mistake. Henceforward we will endeacour to banish from our memories the names of Milton, Shakespeare, Robert Burns, and Tom Moore. We will condemn to annihilation, picture, bust, and statue of our too long worshipped idols, and in their frames or on their pedestals we will place the image and likenes of Walt Whitman, as he appears in the frontispiece of his book:—
"A gentleman in his shirt-sleeves, with one hand in a pocket of his pantaloons, and his wide awake cocked with a dammee-sir air over his forehead."

We append an extract or two from his incomprable poem:—
"Do you guess I have some intricate purpose?
Well I have * * * for the April rain has, and the
mica on the side of a rock has.
Do you take it I would astonish?
Does the daylight astonish? or the early redstart twit-
teringtwittering through the woods?
Do I astonish more than they>
This hour I tell things in condifence,
I might not tell everybody but I will tell you.
Who goes there! hankering, gross, mystical, nude?
How is it I extract srength from the beef I eat?
What is a man anyhow? What am I? and what are
you?
All I mark as my own you shall offest it with your own,
Else it were time lost listening to me.
I do not snivel that snivel the world over,
That moths are vacuums and the ground but wallow
and filth,
That life is a suck and a sell, and nothing remains at the
end but threadbare crape and tears."

On taking a survey of himself, Mr. Whitman grow so delighted that we begin to apprehend he stands in some danger of the fate of Narcissus:—
I dote on myself * * * there is that lot of me, and
all so luscious,
Each moment and whatever thrills me with joy.
I cannot tell how my ankles bend * * * nor whence
the cause of my faintest wish,
Nor the cause of the friendship I emit * * * I pause
to consider if it really be.
That I eat and drink is spectacle enough for the great
authors and schools,
A morning-glory at my window satisfies me more than
the metaphysics of books.
To behold the daybreak!
The little light fades the immense and diaphanous
shadows,
The air tastes good to my palate.
Hefts of the moving world at innocent gambols, silently
rising, freshly exuding,
Scooting obliquely high and low.
Something I cannot see puts upward libidinous prongs,
Seas of bright juice suffuse heaven.
The earth by the sky staid with * * * the daily close
of their junction,
The heaved challenge from the east that moment over
my head,
The mocking taunt—See then whether you shall be
master!
Dazzling and tremendous how quick the sunrise would
kill me,
If I could not now and always send sunrise out of me.
We also ascend dazzling and tremendous as the sun,
We found our own my soul in the calm and cool of the
daybreak.
My voice goes after what my eyes cannot reach,
With the twirl of my tongue I encompass worlds and
volumes of worlds.
Speech is the twin of my vision * * * it is unequal
to measure itself.
It provokes me forever,
It says sarcastically, Walt, you understand enough * *
why don't you let it out then?
Come now I will not be tantalized * * * you conceive
too much of articulation."
Yes, Walt, that last is not a bad hint, by any means—pray you do not let it pass from you.

In another place we meet with these deep reflections:—
"It is wonderful that I should be immortal! as every
one is immortal,
I know it is wonderful * * * but my eyesight is
equally wonderful * * * and how I was conceived
in my mother's womb is equally wonderful,
And how I was not palpable once but am now * * *
and was born on the last day of May 1819 * * *
and passed from a babe in the creeping trance of
three summers and three winters to articulate and
walk * * * are all equally wondering.
And that I grew six feet high * * * and that I have
become a man thirty-six years old in 1855 * * *
and that I am here anyhow—are all equally won-
derfulwonderful;
And that I can think such thoughts as these is just as
wonderful."
In the last line we entirely agree with the author. So great is our surprise that we are unable to follow him any further.
